Nebaioth
nē-bā'yoth
n. (the firstborn of Ishmael and the Arabian tribe descended from him, whose rams Isaiah sees brought up with acceptance on the altar of the LORD; written also Nebajoth)
From Hebrew Nebayoth, of uncertain sense, connected by some with nabat, to look or behold, and hence heights. The Authorized Version spells the man Nebajoth in Genesis and Chronicles and the tribe Nebaioth in Isaiah; it is one name.

Biblical Definition

Nebaioth is the eldest of the twelve princes of Ishmael: “the firstborn of Ishmael, Nebajoth; and Kedar, and Adbeel, and Mibsam” (Gen 25:13), repeated in the Chronicler's roll (1Ch 1:29). Esau married into the family, taking “Mahalath the daughter of Ishmael Abraham&#39;s son, the sister of Nebajoth, to be his wife” (Gen 28:9) — a marriage made to please his father after he saw that the daughters of Canaan pleased him not, and one of the plainest pictures in Genesis of religion attempted as strategy. The tribe became a people of flocks and tents in the northern Arabian desert, brother-tribe to Kedar, and there Isaiah finds them. In the great chapter of the Gentiles streaming to Zion, the desert clans come not as tribute-payers but as worshippers: “All the flocks of Kedar shall be gathered together unto thee, the rams of Nebaioth shall minister unto thee: they shall come up with acceptance on mine altar, and I will glorify the house of my glory” (Isa 60:7). The sons of Hagar's son bring their beasts to the altar of the God of Abraham, and the sacrifice is accepted. It is a startling promise: the line that went out from the covenant household comes back into the courts of the LORD.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Nebaioth; in sacred history he is the firstborn of Ishmael, and an Arabian tribe of his name whose rams Isaiah sees offered on the altar of God.

expand to see more

NEBAIOTH, n. The firstborn son of Ishmael, written also Nebajoth.

He was one of the twelve princes of the Ishmaelites, by their towns and their castles.

His sister Mahalath was taken to wife by Esau, the son of Isaac.

The tribe of his name dwelt in the Arabian desert, and were keepers of flocks.

Isaiah foretells that the rams of Nebaioth shall come up with acceptance on the altar of the LORD.

Key Scripture

Gen 25:13 — "And these are the names of the sons of Ishmael, by their names, according to their generations: the firstborn of Ishmael, Nebajoth; and Kedar, and Adbeel, and Mibsam,"

Gen 28:9 — "Then went Esau unto Ishmael, and took unto the wives which he had Mahalath the daughter of Ishmael Abraham's son, the sister of Nebajoth, to be his wife."

1Ch 1:29 — "These are their generations: The firstborn of Ishmael, Nebaioth; then Kedar, and Adbeel, and Mibsam,"

Isa 60:7 — "All the flocks of Kedar shall be gathered together unto thee, the rams of Nebaioth shall minister unto thee: they shall come up with acceptance on mine altar, and I will glorify the house of my glory."

Modern Corruption

Isaiah 60 is often read as a promise of national restoration for ethnic Israel with the nations reduced to tributaries. The chapter is a prophecy of the church gathered out of every people, the Gentiles coming not as vassals but as worshippers whose offerings are accepted.

expand to see more

The dispensational reading of Isaiah 60 makes the chapter a description of a future millennial Jerusalem receiving the wealth of subject nations, with the sacrificial language taken as a literal restored temple service. That framework was unknown to the church until the nineteenth century and appears in no Reformation confession. Read the verse as it stands: the rams of Nebaioth minister, and they come up with acceptance on God's altar. These are not tribute animals herded in by a defeated people; they are the offerings of worshippers received by the LORD, from the very stock that went out of Abraham's house with Hagar.

The apostles read such promises as fulfilled in the gathering of the Gentiles into Christ. Paul speaks of his own ministry as a priestly service, “ministering the gospel of God, that the offering up of the Gentiles might be acceptable, being sanctified by the Holy Ghost” (Rom 15:16) — which is Isaiah 60:7 in New Testament dress. Peter tells scattered believers they are “an holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God by Jesus Christ” (1Pe 2:5). One altar remains and one sacrifice has been offered upon it; what the flocks of Kedar and the rams of Nebaioth prefigure is desert tribes brought near by the blood of Christ and worshipping with the household they were once outside of.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Nebayoth (H5032), Nebaioth; Yishma'e'l (H3458), Ishmael; Qedar (H6938), Kedar; ratson (H7522), acceptance, good pleasure; sharath (H8334), to minister, serve.

expand to see more

Hebrew Nebayoth (H5032) — Nebaioth; the firstborn of Ishmael and his tribe.

Hebrew Yishma'e'l (H3458) — Ishmael; the father of the twelve princes.

Hebrew Qedar (H6938) — Kedar; the brother-tribe named with him in Isaiah.

Hebrew ratson (H7522) — acceptance; the word of a sacrifice received.

Hebrew sharath (H8334) — to minister; used of the rams that serve the altar.

Usage

"“The firstborn of Ishmael, Nebajoth” — a prince of the desert in Abraham's line."

"“The sister of Nebajoth, to be his wife” — Esau's attempt to please his father by marriage."

"“The rams of Nebaioth shall minister unto thee” — the outsiders brought in as worshippers."
